We discuss the problem of a possible remagnetization but consider that this direction of magnetization gives a good approximation for the palaeolatitude of the Lhasa block during Middle to late Cretaceous time. Results from more recent Tibetan formations are also presented: late Cretaceous to Palaeocene sediments and volcanics give a lower palaeolatitude of 10"N and but more recent andesites have emplaced about 30"N, close to the present-day latitude. An interpretation is proposed whereby the Lhasa block, which was a part of Asia in the early Cretaceous, has undergone first a southward motion accompanied by an anticlockwise rotation and then, after the Palaeocene, a northwar

to the Takena formation with a thickness of about 1OOOm. The age of this series spans from Albian-Cenonianian at the base to an unknown age at the top. The Gangdise plutonic belt intrudes the folded Mesozoic series. The folded Takena and older formations are overlain unconformably by red conglomerates with an intercalation of tuffs and thick volcanics (Lingzizong formation). The Breggia gorge (Ticino, Switzerland) provides a continuous outcrop of Mesozoic limestones covering the time between the Lower Jurassic and Upper Cretaceous. The Jurassic section from the Lower Pliens- bachian to Aalenian is well dated by ammonites. The limestones of these stages are a good quality recorder of the polarity of the geomagnetic field during this time interval. More than 500 cores have been drilled along a 120m thick section with a median distance between cores of about 20cm. Detailed thermal and af demagnetization and further rock magnetic studies were used to determine the characteristic NRM direction for each sample. Initial NRM intensities and low field susceptibilities reflect variations in oxidation potential and sedimentation rate during carbonate deposition. The Breggia section covers an estimated 12 Myr of Lower to Middle Jurassic time during which more than 60 distinct reversals of the geomagnetic field are recorded. This corresponds to a comparatively high mean reversal frequency of about 5 reversals Myr-’. The Breggia polarity zonation can be correlated with the nearby section at Alpe Turati (Como, Italy) and comparable polarity pat

cy of about 5 reversals Myr-’. Introduction The development of cryogenic and digital fluxgate magnetometers, which allow rapid and accurate measurement of weakly magnetized rock sequences such as limestones or deep-sea sediments, has resulted in a proliferation of magnetostratigraphic investigations. Many of these studies have concentrated on Late Cretaceous or Palaeogene strata (e.g. Lowrie & Alvarez 1977; LaBrecque et al. 1981 ; Lowrie et al. 1982) and excellent correlation between magnetostratigraphic polarity intervals and Cainozoic marine magnetic anomalies has been obtained. However, the correlation of the Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous ‘M-sequence’ of marine anomalies (Larson & Pitman 1972) and the significance and duration of the Jurassic magnetic quiet interval is not so clear-cut. The dating of the beginning and end of the M-sequence of oceanic anomalies is still imprecise. Larson & Hilde (1975) estimated the age of the oldest M-anomalies at about 153 Myr on the basis of basal sediment ages in 706 DSDP hole

nsive viscous remagnetization (Lowrie &Kent 1978). Detailed palaeomagnetic studies of continuously deposited Jurassic sections now exposed on land may establish the nature of the Jurassic quiet zone and also set time constraints on its duration. McElhinny & Burek (1971) concluded on the basis of the available data that normal geomagnetic polarity predominated during the Jurassic with a mixed polarity interval starting at about the Oxfordian/Kimmeridgian boundary. Although this picture was not very accurate because of the poor stratigraphic control of the data used, it did not change appre- ciably for some time (Creer 1971 ; Johnson, Nairn & Peterson 1972; Pechersky & Khramov 1973 ; Irving & Pullaiah 1976). It is usually difficult to obtain accurate age control in continental deposits, but high quality biostratigraphic zonation is often found in marine limestone sequences. Polarity patterns derived from Late Jurassic limestone sequences in the Southern Alps (Ogg 1981; Channell, Ogg & Lowrie 1982a) suggest that the oldest of the M-sequence anomalies (M-25) has an age close to the Oxfordian/Kimmeridgian boundary. Oxfordian limestones in Franconia (Southern Germany) are normally magnetized (Heller 1977). A Lower Jurassic Pliensbachian pelagic limestone section from Hunga

These limestones correspond litho- and biostratigraphically (Wiedenmayer 1980) to the Morbio member of the Breggia section. The Jurassic section from the Lower Pliens- bachian to Aalenian is well dated by ammonites. The limestones of these stages are a good quality recorder of the polarity of the geomagnetic field during this time interval. More than 500 cores have been drilled along a 120m thick section with a median distance between cores of about 20cm. Detailed thermal and af demagnetization and further rock magnetic studies were used to determine the characteristic NRM direction for each sample. Initial NRM intensities and low field susceptibilities reflect variations in oxidation potential and sedimentation rate during carbonate deposition. Introduction The development of cryogenic and digital fluxgate magnetometers, which allow rapid and accurate measurement of weakly magnetized rock sequences such as limestones or deep-sea sediments, has resulted in a proliferation of magnetostratigraphic investigations. Many of these studies have concentrated on Late Cretaceous or Palaeogene strata (e.g. Lowrie & Alvarez 1977; LaBrecque et al. 1981 ; Lowrie et al. 1982) and excellent correlation between magnetostratigraphic polarity intervals and Cainozoic marine magnetic anomalies has been obtained. However, the correlation of the Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous ‘M-sequence’ of marine anomalies (Larson & Pitman 1972) and the significance and duration of the Jurassic magnetic quiet interval is not so clear-cut. The dating of the beginning and end of the M-sequence of oceanic anomalies is still imprecise. Larson & Hilde (1975) estimated the age of the oldest M-anomalies at about 153 Myr on the basis of basal sediment ages in 706 DSDP holes. The lack of prominent oceanic magnetic lineations older than this time limit defines a Jurassic magnetic quiet zone which

Geological setting and sampling The Cab0 de Penas region lies on the North Coast of Spain where the northern limb of the Asturian arc is truncated by the sea. In the cliffs from Cab0 de Penas towards the south- east (Fig. 1) an almost complete succession exists from Lower Ordovician till Lower Carboniferous (Truyols & Julivert 1976). The ‘Barrios’ quartzite is overlain by Ordovician shales, with an intercalation of volcanic material in the lower part. Above, the Ordovician ’ series end up with a volcano-detritic succession, including basaltic lavas in the upper part. Then, there is an uninterrupted period of sedimentation up to Early Carboniferous times, with large amounts of fossils giving well-determined stratigraphical ages. Several periods of red sedimentation occur in the sequence. In particular the Siluro-Devonian ‘Furada’ sandstone (called San Pedro elsewhere) is associated with iron ores and has not been sampled because it is unlikely that these complex ores will yield usful palaeomagnetic information. The whole area has been folded by Hercynian deformation and has a general NE-SW trending synclinal shape. Locally, the strata are strongly deformed (Julivert 1976)

Late Devonian-Early Carboniferous sedimentary samples reveal a pre- or syntectonic Carboniferous remanent magnetization similar to the secondary one of the volcanic samples. A soft post-tectonic component appears also in few samples, for which a Late Carboniferous age is inferred. Comparison of the Carboniferous remanent magnetizations and structural parameters suggests that in a late stage of the deformation, the sites have undergone minor rotations around a vertical axis. A 'strike correction' is therefore proposed to take such an effect into account. The average of the corrected mean-site directions (D = 178", I= 19', og5 = 9") is considered to be a good approximation of the Early or Middle Carboniferous palaeomagnetic direction in Asturia. Geological setting and sampling The Cab0 de Penas region lies on the North Coast of Spain where the northern limb of the Asturian arc is truncated by the sea. In the cliffs from Cab0 de Penas towards the south- east (Fig. 1) an almost complete succession exists from Lower Ordovician till Lower Carboniferous (Truyols & Julivert 1976). The ‘Barrios’ quartzite is overlain by Ordovician shales, with an intercalation of volcanic material in the lower part. Above, the Ordovician ’ series end up with a volcano-detritic succession, including basaltic lavas in the upper part. Then, there is an uninterrupted period of sedimentation up to Early Carboniferous times, with large amounts of fossils giving well-determined stratigraphical ages. Several periods of red sedimentation occur in the sequence. In particular the Siluro-Devonian ‘Furada’ sandstone (called San Pedro elsewhere) is associated with iron ores and has not been sampled because it is unlikely that these complex ores will yield usful palaeomagnetic information. The whole area has been folded by Hercynian deformation and has a general NE-SW trending synclinal shape. Locally, the strata are strongly deformed (Julivert 1976)

The Assynt district is centred on a series of thrusted Cambrian sediments between the Lewisian fore- land to the west and the Moine schists to the east. The Assynt igneous suite comprises two major intrusions, the Borrolan and Loch Ailsh centres (Fig. l), and a complex of dykes and sills. The Assynt district is centred on a series of thrusted Cambrian sediments between the Lewisian fore- land to the west and the Moine schists to the east. The Assynt igneous suite comprises two major intrusions, the Borrolan and Loch Ailsh centres (Fig. l), and a complex of dykes and sills. The Ben Loyal igneous complex lies some 30 km north of Assynt and intrudes Moine metasediments. Exposure is poor, especially of the outer phases, for which sampling was limited to the river sections, a quarry and isolated exposures in the peaty lowland. A total of 21 sites were drilled, of which 10 were in the inner phase (Fig. 2). The Loch Ailsh intrusion consists of a variety of broadly uniform leuco-syenites which are well exposed, and a total of six sites were drilled. Lamprophyric dykes and sills exposed along the road and along the shore of Loch Assynt, north of Borrolan, were sampled at nine sites. The Achmelvich dyke was sampled at the coast near Lochinver. It is petrographically similar to ledmorite suggesting a common mag matic origin (Sabine 1953). The Ben Loyal syenite complex comprises three distinct centres of varying grain size and composition. The coarse rock of Ben Loyal itself was sampled at one site, eight sites were drilled in the finer-grained, most mafic Cnoc nan Cuilean intrusion, including two sites in cross-cutting aplite dykes. It is possible (but unlikely) that the palaeomagnetic direction corresponds to a later, post-thrust remagnetization rather than to the original cooling of the body. Multicomponent remanences of normal and reversed polarity have been recognized. Comparison of this apparent polar wander path with the estab- lished path for Britain throws new light on the sequence of thrusting and magmatic activity in the NW Highlands and precludes large-scale (5 1500 km) movement along the Great Glen Fault later than the Ordovician. The data emphasize previously p

these British Ordovician-Silurian data and the contemporary North American data on conventional north Atlantic reconstructions (e.g. Bullard, Everett & Smith 1965) suggesting that an even larger tectonic discontinuity existed between Britain and the North American craton margin. Van der Voo & Scotese (1982) have argued that large (- 2000km) post-Caledonian movement along the Great Glen Fault could account for these discrepancies. Further, in the Devonian the British data are not only discordant with North American data, but also with those from the Baltic region. As a contribution to the enhancement of the database, which is a prerequisite to the solution of these problems, intrusive rocks in the thrust belt marginal to the deformed Caledonides and adjacent to the stable foreland have been studied palaeomagnetically and the results are reported in this paper. They have all been regarded as of Ordovician age although direct evidence of this is only available for some of them. Figure 1. Distribution of the major alkaline intrusions in NW Scotland. The major nappes are also shown (after Parsons 1972). Briden Department ofEurth Sciences, University of Leeds, Leeds LS2 9JT Received 1983 February 28; in original form 1982 October 1 I Summary. A detailed thermal demagnetization study has been carried out on a number of syenitic intrusions from north of the Great Glen Fault in Scotland. Multicomponent remanences of normal and reversed polarity have been recognized. These define a series of palaeomagnetic poles from which an Ordovician to Silurian apparent polar wander path for northern Scotland is deduced. Comparison of this apparent polar wander path with the estab- lished path for Britain throws new light on the sequence of thrusting and magmatic activity in the NW Highlands and precludes large-scale (5 1500 km) movement along the Great Glen Fault later than the Ordovician. The Assynt district is centred on a series of thrusted Cambrian sediments between the Lewisian fore- land to the west and the Moine schists to the east. The Assynt igneous suite comprises two major intrusions, the Borrolan and Loch Ailsh centres (Fig. l), and a complex of dykes and sills. The Ben Loyal igneous complex lies some 30 km north of Assynt and intrudes Moine metasediments. Additionally, a small collection was made from the Achmelvich dyke intruding Lewisian gneisses on the stable Caledonian foreland some 20 km west of Assynt. The multicomponent remanences found in these rocks will be discussed in relation to the timing and scale of local thrusting as well as in relation to the larger scale plate movements associated with Caledonian orogenesis. 2 Geology Almost all the successful palaeomagnetic studies on the Scottish Lower Palaeozoic have been made on dioritic, andesitic, basaltic and ultrabasic igneous rocks. Many of the more acid rocks are palaeomagnetically unstable, e.g. Newer Granites of Garabal Hill (Briden 1970) and Criffel-Dalbeattie (S. J. Kneen, unpublished data). The subjects of the present study are mainly alkaline intrusive rocks, although composition varies considerably within and between the complexes. Chemical and isotopic age data suggest a genetic relationship to the Newer Granite suite (Turnell 1982). The Sole, Ben More, Glencoul and Assynt thrusts form an imbricate series which youngs to the west (Elliot & Johnson 1980). The Moine Thrust overrides the other nappes from the east and it may be that this difference in geometry of the Moine nappe is related to the Assynt intrusions having already been emplaced in the imbricate pile. Briden Department ofEurth Sciences, University of Leeds, Leeds LS2 9JT Received 1983 February 28; in original form 1982 October 1 I Summary. A detailed thermal demagnetization study has been carried out on a number of syenitic intrusions from north of the Great Glen Fault in Scotland. Multicomponent remanences of normal and reversed polarity have been recognized. These define a series of palaeomagnetic poles from which an Ordovician to Silurian apparent polar wander path for northern Scotland is deduced. Comparison of this apparent polar wander path with the estab- lished path for Britain throws new light on the sequence of thrusting and magmatic activity in the NW Highlands and precludes large-scale (5 1500 km) movement along the Great Glen Fault later than the Ordovician. The data emphasize previously published discrepancies between the apparent polar wander paths of Britain, Baltica and Laurentia and are con- sistent with the suggestion that Britain was among a set of intracratonic microplates which underwent complicated, distinct movements throughout the Caledonian orogeny. 1 Introduction

A detailed thermal demagnetization study has been carried out on a number of syenitic intrusions from north of the Great Glen Fault in Scotland. Multicomponent remanences of normal and reversed polarity have been recognized. These define a series of palaeomagnetic poles from which an Ordovician to Silurian apparent polar wander path for northern Scotland is deduced. Comparison of this apparent polar wander path with the estab- lished path for Britain throws new light on the sequence of thrusting and magmatic activity in the NW Highlands and precludes large-scale (5 1500 km) movement along the Great Glen Fault later than the Ordovician. Exposure is poor, especially of the outer phases, for which sampling was limited to the river sections, a quarry and isolated exposures in the peaty lowland. A total of 21 sites were drilled, of which 10 were in the inner phase (Fig. 2). The Loch Ailsh intrusion consists of a variety of broadly uniform leuco-syenites which are well exposed, and a total of six sites were drilled. Lamprophyric dykes and sills exposed along the road and along the shore of Loch Assynt, north of Borrolan, were sampled at nine sites. The Achmelvich dyke was sampled at the coast near Lochinver. It is petrographically similar to ledmorite suggesting a common mag matic origin (Sabine 1953). The Ben Loyal syenite complex comprises three distinct centres of varying grain size and composition. 1978a, b, 1979a, b, 1980a) established an apparent polar wander path (apwp) for this part of Europe. This Armorican apwp is one constraint on tectonic models of orogenies such as the Cadomain, Taconic, Caledonian, Acadian and the Hercynian of Late Precambrian and Palaeozoic times which border the Atlantic realm. Although much has been accomplished in relatively few years, the palaeomagnetic record for these times is still just emerging. Polarity ambiguities combined with rapid Precambrian apparent polar wander, dating inaccuracies and a general scarcity of palaeomagnetic data, result in apwp's with a variety of interpretations (McWilliams 1980). To overcome this problem, more high quality data must be collected to both fill gaps in and substantiate the palaeomagnetic record. This study, as part of the cooperative project, was initiated to document the Armorican apwp further and reports palaeomagnetic results from Late Precambrian and Cambrian igneous rocks (time-scale of Van Eysinga 1975) from the 'Armorican Massif. Two lithologies were sampled; the keratophyre tuffs of Trdguier (640 2 12 Myr) and the microgranite dykes of Loguivy (548 2 24Myr) both dated by whole rock Rb-Sr isochrons recalculated with X = 1.42 x 10-"yr-' from Vidal (1976). carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: 1978a, b, 1979a, b, 1980a) established an apparent polar wander path (apwp) for this part of Europe. This Armorican apwp is one constraint on tectonic models of orogenies such as the Cadomain, Taconic, Caledonian, Acadian and the Hercynian of Late Precambrian and Palaeozoic times which border the Atlantic realm. Although much has been accomplished in relatively few years, the palaeomagnetic record for these times is still just emerging. Polarity ambiguities combined with rapid Precambrian apparent polar wander, dating inaccuracies and a general scarcity of palaeomagnetic data, result in apwp's with a variety of interpretations (McWilliams 1980). To overcome this problem, more high quality data must be collected to both fill gaps in and substantiate the palaeomagnetic record. This study, as part of the cooperative project, was initiated to document the Armorican apwp further and reports palaeomagnetic results from Late Precambrian and Cambrian igneous rocks (time-scale of Van Eysinga 1975) from the 'Armorican Massif. Two lithologies were sampled; the keratophyre tuffs of Trdguier (640 2 12 Myr) and the microgranite dykes of Loguivy (548 2 24Myr) both dated by whole rock Rb-Sr isochrons recalculated with X = 1.42 x 10-"yr-' from Vidal (1976). In contrast, the microgranite high-intensity directions show more scatter both between and within sites than the low intensity group, and the high intensity directions show polarity reversals; occasionally even within the same sample (Fig. 10c). Also the decay of the high intensity remanence during demagnetization differs from that of the low intensity group (Fig. 1 lb, c). Low intensity samples have little relative intensity decay at temperatures below 200°C. At higher temperatures the remanence decays at a fairly constant rate as the Curie temperature of magnetite is approached. High intensity samples on the other hand, have large relative intensity drops at temperatures below 200°C and the remanence decay rate varies greatly at different temperatures. The normalized intensity decays rapidly at lower temperatures; then reaches a 'plateau' at intermediate levels, and finally decays rapidly again at temperatures >500°C. Combined with the much steeper high intensity mean direction (200°/50.8"), the above traits indicate a fundamental difference between the two microgranite dyke magnetizations. Samples of the keratophyre tuffs of Trkguier (640 ? 12 Myr) of the Upper Brioverian series, and the microgranite dykes of Loguivy (548 k 24 Myr) have been collected from the north coast of Brittany, France. ian and Palaeozoic times which border the Atlantic realm. Although much has been accomplished in relatively few years, the palaeomagnetic record for these times is still just emerging. Polarity ambiguities combined with rapid Precambrian apparent polar wander, dating inaccuracies and a general scarcity of palaeomagnetic data, result in apwp's with a variety of interpretations (McWilliams 1980). Two late Mesozoic dolerite sills, situated near Agardhbukta on the east coast of Vestspitsbergen and dated radiometrically at 100 k 4 Myr BP, have been sampled in five localities and subjected to detailed mineralogical and rock magnetic studies to determine the direction and origin of their magnetization. Although the sills lie outside the Tertiary orogenic belt, one locality (no. 4) has undergone strong hydrothermal alteration and a small part of another locality (no. 3) has also been affected. A conventional pro- cedure based on examination of Zijderveld diagrams, applied to specimens demagnetized by alternating fields and thermally, yielded similar remanence directions at all five localities, except at the altered part of locality 3. Using a least squares computer method of analysis of step demagnetization data, comparable directions were isolated from all localities, including the altered part of locality 3. Except in this last case, all directions were reversed. her gabbro bodies. They noted in particular that the mean direction from the Boganclogh mass was very different from the Insch mass. This presented a problem as the Boganclogh mass is an extension of the Insch mass, the link between them being buried beneath a veneer of Old Red Sandstone. her gabbro bodies. They noted in particular that the mean direction from the Boganclogh mass was very different from the Insch mass. This presented a problem as the Boganclogh mass is an extension of the Insch mass, the link between them being buried beneath a veneer of Old Red Sandstone. Remanent magnetization directions of 32 dykes and lava flows sampled near Ayacucho, the Peruvian Andes revealed 14.2' f 5.5" counter- clockwise rotation after the Neogene intrusion of this dyke swarm. Palaeo- magnetic results of these rocks and other palaeomagnetic evidences from the Central Andean Mesozoic rocks suggest relatively recent occurrence of the Andean oroclinal bending around the axis at the Peru-Chile border. Introduction Palaeomagnetic studies on the Mesozoic rocks of the Peruvian Andes and northernmost Chile (Heki, Hamano & Kono 1983; Heki 1983; Heki et al. 1984) have revealed post-Cretaceous counter-clockwise rotation of the Peruvian block and oroclinal bending

Chile border. Introduction Palaeomagnetic studies on the Mesozoic rocks of the Peruvian Andes and northernmost Chile (Heki, Hamano & Kono 1983; Heki 1983; Heki et al. 1984) have revealed post-Cretaceous counter-clockwise rotation of the Peruvian block and oroclinal bending of the Central Andes around an axis at the Peru-Chile border (referred to as the Bolivian orocline; Carey 1955). Hayashida er al. (1 984) also showed the counter-clockwise deviated declination of the Eocene red sediments of the Salla Group in the Bolivian Altiplano and suggested that the oroclinal bending is post-Eocene. Palaeomagnetic studies for much younger rock formations will provide important information on the age of the bending of the Central Andes. Here we report the result of a palaeomagnetic investigation on a Neogene dyke swarm near Ayacucho, in the Peruvian Andes. Its mean direction is D = 180" I= 27.5" (k= 18, ag5= 10.5", N= 12 sites). The C is a low coercivity, low blocking temperature overprint of A and B. Its palaeopole, 102"E, 31"N (dp = 6.5", dm = 12"), is unlike post-1300 Precambrian poles for cratonic North America but matches Silurian and late Ordovician poles. 40Ar/39Ar plateau ages of 446 and 447 Ma determined by Lopez-Martinez and York for plagioclases from one of the Cordova samples confirm this age assign- ment. The C magnetization therefore records a previously unrecognized mild thermal or hydrothermal event that occurred in Palaeozoic time, long after the Grenvillian orogeny. Individual samples recorded both an A magnetization with a palaeopole near Australia and a B magnetization with a palaeopole in the equatorial Pacific. The A magnetization was demonstrably older than the B, and the A-B sequence seemed to mark a convergent juncture with the Logan Loop or Keweenawan Track of the Laurentian APWP. McWilliams & Dunlop (1978) hypothesized, however, that the A and B poles form part of a post-orogenic Grenville Track that is younger than any part of the Keweenawan Track. The Hastings Lowlands is one of the few parts of the Grenville from which pre-orogenic magnetizations might possibly be recovered. Early studies were aimed at testing two different views of the ‘Tibetan model’ of the Grenville orogen. Of course, whether a pre-metamorphic magnetization in either of these intrusions would be strictly pre-orogenic depends on whether the Grenvillian collision coincided with the 1150- 1100 Ma event proposed by Baer (1981a) or with the earlier deformational event which predated these intrusions. When a novel C component of magnetization was discovered in the Cordova gabbro (Dunlop et al. 1980), it was suggested on the basis of preliminary results that it might represent a pre-orogenic magnetization, or at any rate a remanence older than any previously uncovered. bout an order of magnitude lower than estimated cooling rates in the Alps over the past few tens of million years (Baer 1981a). For this reason, and because of the concentration of 1100-1 150 Myr old whole-rock Rb/Sr ages in the central part of the Grenville where the structural grain is NNE and oblique to the Grenville Front, Baer favours a compound cooling history with separate thermal events around 1150-1 100 and 950-900 Ma. The Central Metasedimentary Belt containing the Hastings region is one of the areas that should have felt the effects of a penetrative 1150-1 100 Myr event, but the palaeomagnetic data do not bear this out. All palaeopoles so far reported seem to fall in the 1050-820 Myr interval and are very different from 1150-1 100 Ma poles for rocks of the Lake Superior Keweenawan rift sequence (Fig. l), which may be genetically related to the Grenvillian event or events (Donaldson & Irving 1972; Baer 1981 b). The palaeomagnetic observations do not rule out an 1150-1100 Ma event followed by reheating around 1050-1000Ma to a temperature of about 650”6, which would be sufficient to erase all pre-existing magnetization. 40Ar/39Ar stepheating data for the Thanet complex (Berger & York 1981) are compatible with this compound model: one hornblende with an Ar closure tem

by Symons (1978), Irving (1979), Roy & Robertson (1979), Dunlop (1981), Irving & McGlynn (1981) and Park & Emslie (1983). More specialized reviews of the palaeo- magnetism and geochronology of the Hastings-Haliburton region have been given by Dunlop et al. (1980), Dunlop & Schutts (1983) and York (1984). Early studies were aimed at testing two different views of the ‘Tibetan model’ of the Grenville orogen. In the first view, the Grenvillian analogue of the Himalayan collision zone would lie near the southern edge of the Grenville Front Tectonic Zone (Fig. 1) and much of the Grenville would be an exotic terrane, with a pre-collisional apparent polar wander path (APW) different from that of the remainder of Laurentia. In the other view, ‘Grenvillia’ and ‘Interior Laurentia’ form part of a single plate and the collisional zone lies to the SE of both. Of course, whether a pre-metamorphic magnetization in either of these intrusions would be strictly pre-orogenic depends on whether the Grenvillian collision coincided with the 1150- 1100 Ma event proposed by Baer (1981a) or with the earlier deformational event which predated these intrusions. When a novel C component of magnetization was discovered in the Cordova gabbro (Dunlop et al. 1980), it was suggested on the basis of preliminary results that it might represent a pre-orogenic magnetization, or at any rate a remanence older than any previously uncovered. The detailed results presented in this paper show that this speculation was wrong. The C magnetization is a low-temperature Silurian or late Ordovician overprint, dated at 445-450 Ma by 40Ar/39Ar on plagioclase (Lopez-Martinez & York 1983). This is the first palaeomagnetic evidence for a possible ‘echo’ in the Crenville of Acadian-Caledonian events in the Appalachian Orogen. For this reason, and because of the concentration of 1100-1 150 Myr old whole-rock Rb/Sr ages in the central part of the Grenville where the structural grain is NNE and oblique to the Grenville Front, Baer favours a compound cooling history with separate thermal events around 1150-1 100 and 950-900 Ma. More specialized reviews of the palaeo- magnetism and geochronology of the Hastings-Haliburton region have been given by Dunlop et al. (1980), Dunlop & Schutts (1983) and York (1984). Received 1984 November 9; in original form 1984 July 23 Summary. The Cordova gabbro of southern Ontario intrudes 1300 Myr old volcanic rocks of the Hastings Lowlands in the Grenville Structural Province. Three distinct vector magnetizations (A, B and C) have been isolated, using a combination of stable endpoints, subtracted vectors from orthogonal vector plots and converging remagnetization circles. The A magnetization, with mean direction D = 294" I = - 55.5" (k = 42, ag5 = 5.5", N= 18 sites), is a high coercivity, high blocking temperature remanence recorded by 49 samples. The B magnetization was isolated in 33 samples and has a mean direction D = 305.5"1= - 1 .5" (k = 24, ag5 = 9.5", N= 11 sites). B has lower coerci- vities and blocking temperatures than A where the two are superimposed. The A and B palaeopoles, 151"E, 10.5"S (dp = 6", dm = 8") and 165.5" E, 24"N (dp = So, dm = 9.5"), fall on the Grenville Track around 900 and 820 Ma respectively. The A and B magnetizations thus date from uplift and cooling following the Grenvillian orogeny. The third magnetization, the C component, has been isolated in 23 samples. I

or hornblendes from the Thanet and Cordova gabbros (Berger & York 1981; Lopez-Martinez & York 1983) intensified the search. Of course, whether a pre-metamorphic magnetization in either of these intrusions would be strictly pre-orogenic depends on whether the Grenvillian collision coincided with the 1150- 1100 Ma event proposed by Baer (1981a) or with the earlier deformational event which predated these intrusions. When a novel C component of magnetization was discovered in the Cordova gabbro (Dunlop et al. 1980), it was suggested on the basis of preliminary results that it might represent a pre-orogenic magnetization, or at any rate a remanence older than any previously uncovered. The detailed results presented in this paper show that this speculation was wrong. The C magnetization is a low-temperature Silurian or late Ordovician overprint, dated at 445-450 Ma by 40Ar/39Ar on plagioclase (Lopez-Martinez & York 1983). This is the first palaeomagnetic evidence for a possible ‘echo’ in the Crenville of Acadian-Caledonian events in the Appalachian Orogen. Forty-eight specimens from Ratagan, dated at 415 Itr 5 Ma, gave a mean direc- tion: D= 8", I= - 32", and a palaeomagnetic south pole: 1S0S, 346"E (6p= 5", Fm=9"). Twenty-eight specimens from Comrie, dated at 40855 Ma, gave a mean direction: D = 75", I= - 30", and a palaeomagnetic south pole: 6"S, 287"E(6p = 4", 6m = 7"). These results have been compared with the established apparent polar wander path (APWP) for Britain. The Ratagan pole improves the reliability of the APWP but doubt remains as to whether the primary magnetization from Comrie represents a true late Silurian direction or whether it has been affected by post-cooling rotation, possibly associated with the nearby Highland Boundary Fault. It was initiated during the late Jurassic or Early Cretaceous at the commencement of rifting between Australia and Antarctica. During its early and middle histories the Otway Basin was an intracratonic trough, and accumulated great thicknesses of continental sediments. With the separation of Australia and Antarctica in the Late Cretaceous, the Basin became marginal

North Rankin 1 was drilled into a major structural element on the western edge of the Dampier Sub-basin - the Rankin Platform. This platform consists of large fault blocks, which were formed during the mid-Mesozoic extensional phase and have been subsequently draped by sediments. Except for subsidence the Sub-basin appears to have been tectonically quiescent throughout the Tertiary (Powell 1976). 5 Sampling units and results 5.1 OTWAY GROUP The Otway Group is an Early Cretaceous continental sequence of sandstones, siltstones and minor coal seams. The sediments are predominantly volcaniclastic. The source, or sources, of the volcanic component remain unknown. The minimum age of the Otway Group is constrained by fission track dates on the volcanic detrital components, which range from 126 to 103 Ma (Gleadow & Duddy 1980). The extreme freshness of this detritus, as observed in thin sections, suggests that erosion and deposition had closely followed volcanism. e been carried out on one Cretaceous and five Cenozoic sedimentary sequences of Australia; of those, one is in the Carnarvon Basin of north-western Australia, and the others are in the Otway Basin of south-eastern Australia. The new results are used together with those published previously to define a revised late Mesozoic-Cenozoic apparent polar wander path for Australia. This path differs from earlier, basalt-derived paths by the absence of a large westward excursion and zig-zag irregularities. It is characterized instead by a substantially straight Cenozoic trajectory, a sharp bend in the Late Cretaceous, and a non-uniform rate of apparent polar wander. The early Tertiary segment of the new path lies north of the original paths, thus eliminating a discrepancy that has been noted previously between the Indian and Australian palaeomagnetic data (Luyendyk & Rennick, Peirce and Klootwyk & Peirce). A re-examination of the original data suggests that this discrepancy, as well as two others in the Australian results, may have been caused principally by incomplete time-averaging of remanence directions, because the volcanics on which the results were based had been extruded episodically. In 1970 Wilson pointed out that secular variations are not necessarily cancelled by averaging between successive lava flows, because groups of flows can be extruded over short periods of time. In Wilson's study of Tertiary lavas of Northern Ireland, 32 flows in a sequence of 54 appeared to have been extruded in four brief episodes. Brief periods of basalt extrusion have also been reported from other parts of the world, such as the Stoddart Formation in New Zealand (Evans 1970); Steen Mountains in the USA (Watkins & Baksi 1974); and some Hawaiian lavas (McWilliams, Holcomb & Champion 1982). Most of the Australian Cenozoic poles had been determined by measurements on one principal extinct volcano, supplemented by fewer measurements on other volcanoes. Thus, four out of six poles on the latest basalt-derived path are based primarily on measurements of the Barrington, Liverpool, Nandewar and Tweed volcanoes. The first three of these, like the lavas reported by Wilson (1970), appear to have successive flows with similar remanence directions. Data transfer between widely different localities is, however, strictly valid only if the geomagnetic field can be adequately represented by a geocentric axial dipole, i.e. without higher-order spherical harmonic terms (e.g. Idnurm 1985). Available evidence suggests that for the Cenozoic era such a model is only approximately valid (e.g. Merrill & McElhinny 1983). Embleton (1981) has used the remaneke directions of Australian weathered profiles to define a new, although undated, Cenozoic pole trajectory. These two paths differ from each other in detail, but agree on the absence of zigzags and any pronounced westward excursion. In each case the authors emphasize that their respective paths are tentative. It has become increasingly important to eliminate errors in the Australian pole path. Palaeomagnetic measurements have been carried out on one Cretaceous and five Cenozoic sedimentary sequences of Australia; of those, one is in the Carnarvon Basin of north-western Australia, and the others are in the Otway Basin of south-eastern Australia. In 1970 Wilson pointed out that secular variations are not necessarily cancelled by averaging between successive lava flows, because groups of flows can be extruded over short periods of time. In Wilson's study of Tertiary lavas of Northern Ireland, 32 flows in a sequence of 54 appeared to have been extruded in four brief episodes. Brief periods of basalt extrusion have also been reported from other parts of the world, such as the Stoddart Formation in New Zealand (Evans 1970); Steen Mountains in the USA (Watkins & Baksi 1974); and some Hawaiian lavas (McWilliams, Holcomb & Champion 1982). Most of the Australian Cenozoic poles had been determined by measurements on one principal extinct volcano, supplemented by fewer measurements on other volcanoes. Thus, four out of six poles on the latest basalt-derived path are based primarily on measurements of the Barrington, Liverpool, Nandewar and Tweed volcanoes. The first three of these, like the lavas reported by Wilson (1970), appear to have successive flows with similar remanence directions. North Rankin 1 was drilled into a major structural element on the western edge of the Dampier Sub-basin - the Rankin Platform. The Jurassic Scisti Silicei Formation forms part of the Lagonegro superimposed tectonic units I and I1 that are thought to represent the axial and internal margins of the Mesozoic Lagonegro Basin, prior to nappe formation. Sampling was carried out in the lower (Lagonegro) and upper (Pignola) nappes in two differently oriented anticlines. Single and multi- component magnetizations are present. Isothermal remanence acquisition rates show that magnetite and haematite are present which, in most hgonegro specimens, show the same direction of magnetization. Comparison of the palaeomagnetic directions with those from Jurassic rocks on the stable African craton indicates a 147" anticlockwise rotation of the lower nappe which is similar to 139" previously reported for the upper nappe at Vietri di Potenza. The same comparisons show a 44" clockwise rotation of the upper nappe at Pignola. These results suggest that the doubled nappe structures, sampled some 50 km apart, resulted from their emplacement by translation with little rotation prior to the ope

carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: conclusions The steep inclinations which predominate in the Lagonegro locality, and are of restricted occurrence in the Pignola area, are well defined and of consistent reversed polarity. This suggests that they were acquired in a reversed geomagnetic field prior to folding. However, such an inclination is inconsistent with any possible post-Triassic palaeolatitude for this area (c. 25-30') or with any direction which could have been acquired during a tilt at some specific time during the nappe development and emplacement. Thus these directions, while clearly defined, remain of unknown origin. The sites from Pignola which show single component magnetization are characterized by a south-westerly declination, intermediate negative inclination, which is carried by magnetite, while the north-westerly direction, of intermediate positive inclination, is characteristic of the high temperature component of the multicomponent sites which contain magnetite, specularite and pigmentary haematite. The identification of the SW component in some of the multicomponent sites, together with the more complex mineralogy, indicates that the NW direction probably represents a later acquired magnetiz- ation than the SW directed component. Samples have been taken systematically through the intrusive sequence for the three centres which form the Tertiary central intrusive ring complex. Palaeomagnetic measurements show that all the units are reversely magnetized as are the earlier lavas - an extension of those of Mull and Morvern - which they intrude. This is in contrast to Mull. Skye and Arran, where the igneous sequences have been shown to span at least three polarity intervals, but is similar to Rhum where the only normal units are a few late dykes. Since Rhum and Ardnamuchan both lie on the dyke swarm which passes through Muck, the two complexes are considered to be closely related. Palaeomagnetic measurements show that all the units are reversely magnetized as are the earlier lavas - an extension of those of Mull and Morvern - which they intrude. This is in contrast to Mull. Skye and Arran, where the igneous sequences have been shown to span at least three polarity intervals, but is similar to Rhum where the only normal units are a few late dykes. Since Rhum and Ardnamuchan both lie on the dyke swarm which passes through Muck, the two complexes are considered to be closely related. If the Ardnamurchan central complex was formed in a single reversed interval the total duration of igneous activity was less than 3 Myr. Rocks from the Massif de la Serre in the French Jura (latitude: 47.3"N longitude: 5.6"E) belonging to an ignimbritic assemblage dominated by vitrophyric rhyolites, and whose age of formation is probably Permian (Autunian to Saxonian) have been studied by applying thermal and alter- nating field demagnetization. The characteristic magnetization has a mean direction derived from 89 samples of D = 170", I = - 16", k = 26.2", 01~~ = 3" and a corresponding north palaeopole at 41"N, 172"E, AgS = 5". The pole, which is very close to the Permian European poles, can thus be considered as a new contribution. Some samples are found to carry a unique normal polarity magnetization, others carry both normal and reverse polarities. It therefore seems that, similar to Permian series in the USSR, these west European rocks have registered a normal event in the Kiaman interval. From a structural point of view, we may conclude that during the Alpine tectonic phases the Massif de la Serre has not been subjected to substantial rotation. e palaeomagnetic data are needed, particularly from Spitsbergen. After the Caledonian activity and its rejuvenation during the Upper Devonian (Harland 1969; Birkenmajer 1981), Spitsbergen remained tectonically stable until the opening of North Atlantic and Arctic basins, which caused the West Spitsbergen orogeny along the western edge of the island. As the Variscan orogeny hardly affected south Spitsbergen, palaeomagnetic studies may provide data undisturbed by the Variscan activity. Devonian rocks in Spitsbergen occur in two N-S trending grabens exposed in the northern part of the island and in a smaller one in the south. The Old Red Sandstone molasse, of late orogenic origin, was deposited in these grabens. The oldest sediments are in the north of the island and the most widespread deposits belong to the Wood Bay Formation. This formation consists of continental red coloured sandstones with siltstones and shales of Siegenian- Emsian age. There are two main sources of clastics (Friend & Moody-Stuard 1972). Key words: palaeomagnetism, K-Ar ages, Cretaceous, Portugal, tectono- magmatic implications Introduction Post-Hercynian palaeomagnetic data from Spain and Portugal have traditionally been associated with a counterclockwise rotational opening of the Bay of Biscay (Schwarz 1963; Van Dongen 1967; Girdler 1968; Watluns & Richardson 1968a; Van der Voo 1969; Stauffer & Tarling 197 1 ; Van der Voo & Zijderveld 197 1 ; Storetvedt 1973; Van den Berg 1979), and the Upper Cretaceous has repeatedly been considered as the time during which Iberia detached from the European plate (Van der Voo 1969; Stauffer & Tarling 1971 ; Williams 1975; Van den Berg 1979; Boillot 1984). However, despite the many geophysical and geo- logical studies, the tectonic setting of Iberia is far from clear, and in a recent discussion on the tectonic evolution of the Pyrenees (see McCaig & Wickham 1984) the need for further detailed palaeomagnetic studies of the Cretaceous of Iberia was stressed. The present paper contributes to this task, reporting new palaeomagnetic and radiometric results from the late Cretaceous Sintra and Sines intrusive complexes of W. Portugal as well as giving further details on the palaeomagnetic structure of the Lisbon volcanics. The latter formation has previo

The Sines complex, located some 105 km south-southeast of the Sintra hills (see Fig. 1 a) shows several characteristic features similar to the Sintra massif, i.e. elliptical shape, nearly east-west orientation, sub-volcanic ring-structure (Teixeira 1962; Ribeiro 1979) etc. The major part of the complex lies offshore. The subaerial part is largely covered by Quaternary deposits, the exposed rocks constituting only a narrow littoral section. Both on the north and south side of the complex thermal aureoles have been generated in the adjacent sedimentary rocks, causing various types of thermometamorphism (Canilho 1971). The most important petrographic types are gabbro, diorite and syenite. The complex is cut by numerous dykes of varied composition. Radiometric studies (see below) suggest that the Sines intrusive mass formed contemporaneously with the Cab0 da Roca complex. This seems to fit the hypothesis of Ribeiro (1 979) that the Sines and Sintra intrusions are connected by a common strike-slip fracture. These complexes form part of the late Cretaceous alkaline igneous province of Iberia (Rock 1982). K. M. Storetvedt et al. -rnE LISBON VOLCANICS The Lisbon volcanic complex (Fig. 2) is situated east of the Sintra massif, forming a north- south trending belt of isolated volcanic vents, cutting across Cenomanian sedimentary strata, and numerous lava flows alternating with less abundant tuff layers. There is also a dyke net- work, almost exclusively vertical, and a few late stage volcanic vents piercing lava flows. Petrographically, the Lisbon volcanics are mostly composed of basaltic rocks, but hawaiites and mugearites are also present. Coarser grained varieties include ankaramites and ankaratrites, and aphanitic rocks include basanites and basanitoides (Alves et al. 1980). The volcanic complex comprises at least 15 eruptive centres. Their pipes (plugs, necks and breccias) and part of their cones are still visible, forming an almost continuous belt between the Cascais/Oeiras and Mafra/Malveira districts. Key words: palaeomagnetism, K-Ar ages, Cretaceous, Portugal, tectono- magmatic implications Introduction Post-Hercynian palaeomagnetic data from Spain and Portugal have traditionally been associated with a counterclockwise rotational opening of the Bay of Biscay (Schwarz 1963; Van Dongen 1967; Girdler 1968; Watluns & Richardson 1968a; Van der Voo 1969; Stauffer & Tarling 197 1 ; Van der Voo & Zijderveld 197 1 ; Storetvedt 1973; Van den Berg 1979), and the Upper Cretaceous has repeatedly been considered as the time during which Iberia detached from the European plate (Van der Voo 1969; Stauffer & Tarling 1971 ; Williams 1975; Van den Berg 1979; Boillot 1984). However, despite the many geophysical and geo- logical studies, the tectonic setting of Iberia is far from clear, and in a recent discussion on the tectonic evolution of the Pyrenees (see McCaig & Wickham 1984) the need for further detailed palaeomagnetic studies of the Cretaceous of Iberia was stressed. The present paper contributes to this task, reporting new palaeomagnetic and radiometric results from the late Cretaceous Sintra and Sines intrusive complexes of W. Portugal as well as giving further details on the palaeomagnetic structure of the Lisbon volcanics. The latter formation has previo

The Sines complex, located some 105 km south-southeast of the Sintra hills (see Fig. 1 a) shows several characteristic features similar to the Sintra massif, i.e. elliptical shape, nearly east-west orientation, sub-volcanic ring-structure (Teixeira 1962; Ribeiro 1979) etc. The major part of the complex lies offshore. The subaerial part is largely covered by Quaternary deposits, the exposed rocks constituting only a narrow littoral section. Both on the north and south side of the complex thermal aureoles have been generated in the adjacent sedimentary rocks, causing various types of thermometamorphism (Canilho 1971). The most important petrographic types are gabbro, diorite and syenite. The complex is cut by numerous dykes of varied composition. Radiometric studies (see below) suggest that the Sines intrusive mass formed contemporaneously with the Cab0 da Roca complex. This seems to fit the hypothesis of Ribeiro (1 979) that the Sines and Sintra intrusions are connected by a common strike-slip fracture. These complexes form part of the late Cretaceous alkaline igneous province of Iberia (Rock 1982). K. M. There is also a dyke net- work, almost exclusively vertical, and a few late stage volcanic vents piercing lava flows. Petrographically, the Lisbon volcanics are mostly composed of basaltic rocks, but hawaiites and mugearites are also present. Coarser grained varieties include ankaramites and ankaratrites, and aphanitic rocks include basanites and basanitoides (Alves et al. 1980). The volcanic complex comprises at least 15 eruptive centres. Their pipes (plugs, necks and breccias) and part of their cones are still visible, forming an almost continuous belt between the Cascais/Oeiras and Mafra/Malveira districts. The Sines complex, located some 105 km south-southeast of the Sintra hills (see Fig. 1 a) shows several characteristic features similar to the Sintra massif, i.e. elliptical shape, nearly east-west orientation, sub-volcanic ring-structure (Teixeira 1962; Ribeiro 1979) etc. The major part of the complex lies offshore. The subaerial part is largely covered by Quaternary deposits, the exposed rocks constituting only a narrow littoral section. Both on the north and south side of the complex thermal aureoles have been generated in the adjacent sedimentary rocks, causing various types of thermometamorphism (Canilho 1971). The most important petrographic types are gabbro, diorite and syenite. The complex is cut by numerous dykes of varied composition. Radiometric studies (see below) suggest that the Sines intrusive mass formed contemporaneously with the Cab0 da Roca complex. This seems to fit the hypothesis of Ribeiro (1 979) that the Sines and Sintra intrusions are connected by a common strike-slip fracture. These complexes form part of the late Cretaceous alkaline igneous province of Iberia (Rock 1982). K. M. There is also a dyke net- work, almost exclusively vertical, and a few late stage volcanic vents piercing lava flows. Petrographically, the Lisbon volcanics are mostly composed of basaltic rocks, but hawaiites and mugearites are also present. Coarser grained varieties include ankaramites and ankaratrites, and aphanitic rocks include basanites and basanitoides (Alves et al. 1980). The volcanic complex comprises at least 15 eruptive centres. Their pipes (plugs, necks and breccias) and part of their cones are still visible, forming an almost continuous belt between the Cascais/Oeiras and Mafra/Malveira districts. Hence, even the youngest palaeomagnetic component of the Lisbon volcanics (i.e. that directed along or close to the direction of the present axial dipole field) may at least in part pre-date the local tectonic deformation. Therefore, the late Tertiary magnetization should in principle respond positively to structural unfolding provided the pretectonic component constitutes more than 50 per cent of the ‘stable remanence’. This is apparently the case in the study by Van der Voo & Zijderveld (1971). Portugal), and further details on the palaeomagnetic structure of the Lisbon volcanics are reported. The Sintra complex consists of two main intrusive phases having been emplaced in the Upper Cretaceous at around 90 Ma and 75 Ma respectively. The radiometric results show that the Sines complex formed concurrently with the second Sintra magmatism. The early (main) Sintra pluton has a characteristic magnetization of D=358', I = 27' (ag5 = 3.3'). GEOLOGY AND SAMPLING The Archaan greenstone sequence of the Pilbara craton is very diverse, containing most of the rock types found in other greenstone sequences of the world. A detailed description of the succession is given by Hickman and Lipple [1975]. The Warrawoona Group forms the basal, predominantly volcanic assemblage. Relatively thin chart units occur frequently inter- posed between ultramafic-mafic and ultramafic-felsic cycles. The upper part of the succession, the Gorge Creek Group, is predominantly a sedimentary assemblage of banded iron for- mations, argillaceous rocks, and sandstones with subordinate pillow basalt. The layered succession commonly exceeds 15 km in thickness and has been subjected to isoclinal folding. In the area sampled around Marble Bar (Figure 1) the beds are slightly overturned, as is clearly evidenced from the facing of the pillow basalts at the two localities. Greenschist facies metamorphism predominates in most areas. There have been two intervals of granite emplacement, a main one at around 3000 Ma [Campston and/trriens, 1968] and a younger event when the main granite batholiths were intruded by irregular masses of adamellite at around 2600 Ma. It consists basically of an Archaan layered succession or greenstone sequence preserved within several linear and arcuate belts between large oval- shaped granite batholiths (Figure 1). GEOLOGY AND SAMPLING The Archaan greenstone sequence of the Pilbara craton is very diverse, containing most of the rock types found in other greenstone sequences of the world. A detailed description of the succession is given by Hickman and Lipple [1975]. The Warrawoona Group forms the basal, predominantly volcanic assemblage. Relatively thin chart units occur frequently inter- posed between ultramafic-mafic and ultramafic-felsic cycles. The upper part of the succession, the Gorge Creek Group, is predominantly a sedimentary assemblage of banded iron for- mations, argillaceous rocks, and sandstones with subordinate pillow basalt. The layered succession commonly exceeds 15 km in thickness and has been subjected to isoclinal folding. In the area sampled around Marble Bar (Figure 1) the beds are slightly overturned, as is clearly evidenced from the facing of the pillow basalts at the two localities. Greenschist facies metamorphism predominates in most areas. GEOLOGY AND SAMPLING The Archaan greenstone sequence of the Pilbara craton is very diverse, containing most of the rock types found in other greenstone sequences of the world. A detailed description of the succession is given by Hickman and Lipple [1975]. The Warrawoona Group forms the basal, predominantly volcanic assemblage. Relatively thin chart units occur frequently inter- posed between ultramafic-mafic and ultramafic-felsic cycles. The upper part of the succession, the Gorge Creek Group, is predominantly a sedimentary assemblage of banded iron for- mations, argillaceous rocks, and sandstones with subordinate pillow basalt. The layered succession commonly exceeds 15 km in thickness and has been subjected to isoclinal folding. In the area sampled around Marble Bar (Figure 1) the beds are slightly overturned, as is clearly evidenced from the facing of the pillow basalts at the two localities. Greenschist facies metamorphism predominates in most areas. There have been two intervals of granite emplacement, a main one at around 3000 Ma [Campston and/trriens, 1968] and a younger event when the main granite batholiths were intruded by irregular masses of adamellite at around 2600 Ma. METHODS The majority of samples collected were drilled using port- able rock drills and oriented using both magnetic and sun compasses [Embleton, 1979']. The cores were later sliced into specimens of nominal dimensions 2.5 cm diameter x 2.2 cm height, usually yielding two to four specimens per core. Mag- netizations of specimens were measured using an ScT Squid magnetometer or Digico flux gate magnetometers. The latter instruments were only used for magnetic moments greater than approximately 10 -5 emu (10 -8 A m-). Demagnetization of specimens was performed with a three- axis tumbling alternating field (af) device (similar to that de- scribed by Roy et al. [1972]) or less frequently with Schon- stedt GSD-1 af equipment. Most specimens were demagne- tized using a furnace and zero-field coils similar to those de- scribed by McElhinny et al. [1971]. Demagnetization trends from all demagnetized specimens have been examined with the aid of both stereo nets and orthogonal plots [-Zijderveld, 1967]. In this study, particular emphasis has been placed upon the fold test [Graham, 1949] as a means of establishing the timing of magnetizations. We note that while baked con- tact tests are potentially capable of relating magnetizations to original cooling and are often reported as such, definitive ac- counts of the full contact test described by Graham [1949], are rare because the test is intrinsically difficult to implement. Although the fold test is less powerful than the contact test, it is often easy to implement, unless of course sequences are everywhere flat lying or the directions of magnetization and fold axes are parallel. METHODS The majority of samples collected were drilled using port- able rock drills and oriented using both magnetic and sun compasses [Embleton, 1979']. The cores were later sliced into specimens of nominal dimensions 2.5 cm diameter x 2.2 cm height, usually yielding two to four specimens per core. Mag- netizations of specimens were measured using an ScT Squid magnetometer or Digico flux gate magnetometers. The latter instruments were only used for magnetic moments greater than approximately 10 -5 emu (10 -8 A m-). In this study, particular emphasis has been placed upon the fold test [Graham, 1949] as a means of establishing the timing of magnetizations. In some cases, two of these RMs were present in a sample, giving a multicomponent NRM, but usually one of the components dominated the NRM after removal of soft present field overprints. Introduction The composition and structure of the lower continental crust have been inferred mainly from remotely sensed geophysical properties and petrological and geochemical study of xenoliths in diatremes and volcanic pipes [Fountain and Salisbury, 1981]. The key to a better understanding of deep crustal lithologies and structural relationships lies in the study of uplifted zones at ancient convergent plate margins, where erosion of the upper plate has exposed a cross section of the continental crust [Wasilewski and Fountain, 1982; Williams et al., 1985]. Such zones are marked by anomalies in seismic structure, gravity, and aeromagnetics, and typically have a gradational decrease in metamorphic grade away from major fault zones along which uplift took place. The KSZ is a 400-km long, NNE trending belt of dense high-grade gneissic rocks, cutting across the E-W grain of greenschist and amphibolite-grade rocks of the Arcbean Superior P

lift. Late Proterozoic 4øAr/39Ar ages from minerals with low Ar blocking temperatures [Farrar and Archibald, 1985; Hanes, 1985; Lopez-Martinez and York, 1986] suggest a mild reactivation at 1.1-1.0 Ga. Sampling, Measurements, and Analysis Five or more samples oriented by Brunton compass were collected from 15 sites on the Racine and Shawmere traverses. The eight Racine sites (46 samples analyzed) were in tonalites and mafic gneisses, while five of the Shawmere sites (27 samples) were in the anorthosite, and two sites (15 samples) were in gneisses of the southern line. Stepwise alternating field (AF) demagnetization to 100 mT and thermal demagnetization to 600øC were carded out in magnetic shields with standard commercial demagnetizers. Magnetizations were measured with Schonstedt and Digico magnetometers. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: Both magnetic and sun compasses were used to orientate a total of 160 sample-blocks from Itajai, Castro and Bom Jardim Groups from sites shown in Fig. 1. Particulars of sampling sites (which were generally quames and roadcuts) are illustrated in Table 1. Site CA-111, within the Campo Alegre Formation, is a quarry which is cut by a vertical rhyolite dyke 35 cm wide which has been sampled. For the Vargas Formation, each sedimentary sample represents a stratigraphic level. Generally four specimens were cut from each rock sample, making a total of 640 which were measured with a spinner magnetometer. Samples were submitted to AF and thermal demagnetization and practically all the specimens, especially those from the Bom Jardim Group, were given a complete pilot treatment. Magnetizations were analysed with the aid of stereonets, Zijderveld diagrams and intensity curves. Fisher's statistics were used for calculating mean values and precision parameters. Inter., 24: 142—168. Palaeomagnetic results from Precambrian rocks suggest that the geomagnetic field in the Precambrian was similar in major respects to the Recent field, although there is a possibility that reversals were less frequent. Limitations of precision in Proterozoic palaeomagnetic and geochronological data, and inadequate geographic spread of these data, prevent the making of complete Proterozoic continental reconstructions. Nevertheless, where the data are most abundant, Precambrian apparent polar wander (APW) paths can be used in determining the relative movement of cratons and groups of cratons. Relative movement between Africa, Laurentia and Australia during at least part of the Proterozoic seems to be indicated, but the lack of significant differences between the APW paths of several pairs of presently adjacent Proterozoic cratons suggests that some Proterozoic orogenic belts were not formed by the collision of previously widely separated blocks. J. Hale and D. J. Dunlop Geophysics Laboratory, Departments of Geology and Physics University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada M5S 1A7 Abstract. 3.5 Ga old peridotitic komatiites of the Komati formation, Barberton greenstone belt, South Africa have a characteristic NRM (natural remanent magnetization) that is stable during alternating field and thermal demagneti- zation. The thermal nature of this remanence is demonstrated by successful Thellier-type paleo- intensity determinations on some samples in the temperature range 350 to 575øC. The character- istic NRM is an almost total thermal overprint acquired during unroofing and cooling following pervasive greenschist metamorphism at 3470ñ20 Ma. The mean direction of magnetization after cleaning is D=326 ø I=81 ø (k=60, 95=8 ø, N = 7 sites), with a paleopole at 11øS, 21øE (p= m=15ø). The paleopole falls in southern Africa; ancestral southern Africa was therefore in polar latitudes around 3.5 Ga, the same position it occupied in the late Archean and early Proterozoic. roterozoic. Paleofield intensities are about one-half present-day intensities for polar latitudes. A vigorous earth's magnetic field was already in existence in the early Archean, implying that the core had a suitable size, composition and convective flow to support dynamo action. Introduction We report paleomagnetic directional data and paleofield intensities from the Komati forma- tion, Onverwacht group, South Africa. These lavas erupted 3540ñ30 Ma ago (Sm/Nd, Hamilton et al., 1979) and were metamorphosed to green- schist facies shortly afterwards. In 40Ar/39Ar stepheating analyses of metamorphic mineral assemblages from our samples, Lopez-Martinez et al. (1984) have found plateau ages of 3450-3490 Ma. The characteristic magnetization in our study is an almost total thermal overprint dating from this metamorphism. This belt lies parallel to common fault lines in the same area (Härme 1961) and to a deep negative gravi- metric anomaly (Honkasalo 1962) bordering the belt on its SW side. Mikkola and Niini (1966, 1968) divided the zone into three metal- logenic provinces and noticed an abundance of basic (subsilisic) intrusions within the belt associated with the ore bodies. The Haukivesi area The Haukivesi area is located in the south- eastern part of the Raahe—Ladoga zone (Fig. 1). The geology of the area has been described in detail by Hackman (1933), Gaål and Rauha- mäki (1971) and Korsman and Pääjärvi (1980). The area is characterized by highly meta- morphic supracrustal rocks and by hyper- sthene-bearing plutonic rocks with sporadic basic (subsilicic) dykes (Fig. 2). The subracrustal complex consists of garnet-cordierite-sillimanite gneisses, hyper- sthene gneisses and hypersthene amphib- olites. The garnet-cordierite-sillimanite gneisses are migmatized by trondhjemites. The metamorphism of these rocks took place under conditions of granulite facies but, according to Paavola (1976), the pressure was not very high during the recrystallization. Agglomeratic and pillow lava structures in some of the amphibolites and gneisses in the area suggest a volcanic origin for these rocks. The remanent magnetization found in these 112 K. J. On the northwestern side of the Tahkomäki quartzite ridge, in the Jonsa area, northeast of Varpaisjärvi (Fig. 3), the basement differs from other Archean granite gneiss types of Finland particularly in its orthopyroxene content. The rock here is highly metamor- phosed and forms a clearly limited, separate block of basement. It has a high magnetite content and is seen as a strong magnetic anomaly on the aeromagnetic map. The Nilsiä—Varpaisjärvi area North of Kuopio, the boundary between the Svecokarelian rocks and the Archean basement runs subparallel to the Belt (Fig. 1). The Nilsiä—Varpaisjärvi area lies about 50 km north of Kuopio and the majority of the rocks in this area belong to the Archean basement complex. It is divided into two parts by the N-S-trending Proterozoic (Sveco- karelian) Tahkomäki quartzite ridge (Fig. 3). On the eastern side of the quartzite ridge, in the Lake Syväri area, the basement com- prises mainly of banded and migmatitic paragneisses of diverse compo

matitic paragneisses of diverse compositions. These gneisses are quartz dioritic or dioritic in com- position with mica- and hornblende gneiss and amphibolite horizons. Narrow cordierite- gneiss bands also occur. This paragneiss com- plex is weakly magnetized and was not studied paleomagnetically. On the northwestern side of the Tahkomäki quartzite ridge, in the Jonsa area, northeast of Varpaisjärvi (Fig. 3), the basement differs from other Archean granite gneiss types of Finland particularly in its orthopyroxene content. The rock here is highly metamor- phosed and forms a clearly limited, separate block of basement. It has a high magnetite content and is seen as a strong magnetic anomaly on the aeromagnetic map. The remanent magnetization of the rocks of the complex being very high, it is suitable for paleomagnetic investigations. These basement rocks in the Jonsa area are cut by diabase dykes (Fig. 3) running approxi- mately in an E-W or SE-NW direction. The Nilsiä—Varpaisjärvi area North of Kuopio, the boundary between the Svecokarelian rocks and the Archean basement runs subparallel to the Belt (Fig. 1). The Nilsiä—Varpaisjärvi area lies about 50 km north of Kuopio and the majority of the rocks in this area belong to the Archean basement complex. It is divided into two parts by the N-S-trending Proterozoic (Sveco- karelian) Tahkomäki quartzite ridge (Fig. 3). On the eastern side of the quartzite ridge, in the Lake Syväri area, the basement com- prises mainly of banded and migmatitic paragneisses of diverse compo

matitic paragneisses of diverse compositions. These gneisses are quartz dioritic or dioritic in com- position with mica- and hornblende gneiss and amphibolite horizons. Narrow cordierite- gneiss bands also occur. This paragneiss com- plex is weakly magnetized and was not studied paleomagnetically. On the northwestern side of the Tahkomäki quartzite ridge, in the Jonsa area, northeast of Varpaisjärvi (Fig. 3), the basement differs from other Archean granite gneiss types of Finland particularly in its orthopyroxene content. The rock here is highly metamor- phosed and forms a clearly limited, separate block of basement. It has a high magnetite content and is seen as a strong magnetic anomaly on the aeromagnetic map. The remanent magnetization of the rocks of the complex being very high, it is suitable for paleomagnetic investigations. A second set of intersecting dykes occurs in the Nilsiä area (Fig. 3). These dykes are fine- grained, massive and homogeneous. The con- tacts with the wall rock are sharp and apophyses are common. The dykes are from a few centimetres to 4—5 metres wide. Their direction varies between N15°W and N85°W (345°—275°). The dip is subvertical. The mineral composition of these dykes includes plagioclase, quartz, biotite and horn- blende with accessory epidote, sphene, apatite and magnetite. Plagioclase occurs locally as intensely zoned (An 35.25) laths, 1.5—2 mm in size. According to the classification of Streckeisen (1976), these dykes have a tonali- tic or quartz dioritic composition. Paleomagnetic data on the Main Sulphide Ore Belt in Finland are coherent but differ clearly from those obtained on the Archean basement area immediately north of it. The coherent magnetization in ithe Belt could have been caused by (i) axial uplift, (ii) a plate suture along the Belt or (iii) a short-time igneous pulse. The last interpretation is accepted since it agrees with the radiometric age data. Thus the paleomagnetic measurements in the area date the same thermal events as do the radiometric U-Pb age determinations, and the shape of the APW curve is thereby verified. A paleomagnetic pole determined for dykes intersecting the Archean basement block lies off the accepted APW curve which possibly need to be corrected. The magmatic pulse between 1880— 1840 Ma may have been associated with a plate collision or with a deep fluid convection producing the sulphide ore precipitation within the Belt. K. J. On the northwestern side of the Tahkomäki quartzite ridge, in the Jonsa area, northeast of Varpaisjärvi (Fig. 3), the basement differs from other Archean granite gneiss types of Finland particularly in its orthopyroxene content. The rock here is highly metamor- phosed and forms a clearly limited, separate block of basement. It has a high magnetite content and is seen as a strong magnetic anomaly on the aeromagnetic map. The lithology of the area Lithologically, the Belt is not well defined and its borders cannot be drawn exactly. The simplest tectonic model to explain the observed paleomagnetic character of the areas now studied is axial uplift or subsiding of the Belt in relation to the basement com- plex in the northeast. On the northwestern side of the Tahkomäki quartzite ridge, in the Jonsa area, northeast of Varpaisjärvi (Fig. 3), the basement differs from other Archean granite gneiss types of Finland particularly in its orthopyroxene content. The paleomagnetic mea- surements are concentrated on two areas: One is in the central part of the Main Sul- phide Ore Belt in the Haukivesi area, the other is just north of the Belt in the Archean basement complex in the Nilsiä—Varpais- järvi area (Fig. 1). The lithology and paleo- magnetic data obtained will be described and discussed below. Additional paleomagnetic results already available from the north- western end of the Belt and from the Iisalmi area (see Fig. 1) will be included in the Dis- cussion. Radiometric age data and lead iso- tope values will also be considered in drawing conclusions about the origin and evolution of the Belt. The lithology of the area Lithologically, the Belt is not well defined and its borders cannot be drawn exactly. It consists of series of metasediments and meta- volcanics deformed, recrystallized and folded during the Svecokarelian (1800—1900 Ma) orogeny. These schists and gneisses are pene- trated by various of intrusive rocks mainly of synkinematic character. An area typical of the Belt is met with in the southeastern part of the zone in the Haukivesi area (Figs. 1 and 2). INTERPRETATION A major problem during thermal analysis of especially the carbonate specimens was excessive increase in susceptibility and in VRM (Fig. 1.6T, U, V,) at temperatures well above 400°C. This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). It is well known (Dunlop, 1972) that newly formed magnetic phases may acquire a magnetization in absence of an ambient magnetic field, because of exchange coupling with the o

case of carbonate samples with a weak initial intensity which are subsequently further reduced during the demagnetization process, formation of such a secondary magnetic component may make it impossible to determine the primary magnetic component. Most red-bed samples showed an increase in susceptibility (Fig. 1.6R) after prolonged heating at temperatures above 500-6OO”C. A notable exception were red-bed samples from the Parachilna Formation and from the top member of the Billy Creek Formation (Fig. 1.6S, Table 1.4), which showed a significant decrease in susceptibility after heating above 400°C. This may be due to inversion of m~haemite to haematite (Turner and Ixer, 1977). The individual behaviour of the specimens during thermal demagnetiza- tion was variable (Fig. 1.5). It was often found that specimens taken from the same sample showed widely different blocking temperature regions for magnetic components of similar direction. This may partly be due to initial presence of an intimate mixture of authigenic magnetic minerals (Larson and Walker, 1975) further enhanced by a large variability in thermomagnetic properties of the transformed phase upon oxidation (Ryabushkin, 1976). Therefore, I prefer to treat the specimen directions as the fundamental unit for calculation of mean directions

e option available, the method tends to be justified as the obtained mean directions could be interpreted in a meaningful way with respect to the mean early Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic data from Gondwanaland and the tectonic and thermo-chemical history of the region studied. The occasional presence of both normal and reversed polarities of the same magnetic component in the same specimen (Fig. 1.7A), points to a fairly long period of acquisition of the characteristic magnetic component spanning at least the period of one polarity reversal. Such a prolonged acquisition of magnetization may be due to the formation of authigenic oxyhydroxides and haematite during diagenesis, and later dehydration and oxidation due to changes in Eh-Ph conditions and/or tectonic and thermo- chemical effects. For instance, Dijksman (1977) observed in Miocene red clay beds from central Spain that the same magnetic direction resided in both magnetite and a haematite magnetic phase. The latter was acquired with a time lag of several 100.000 yrs due to the effect of changing Eh-Ph condition in the CRM formation process. Dual polarity observations were also made in Billy Creek equivalent beds on Kangaroo Island and in some sequences in the Amadeus Basin (Section III). Cambrian-Early Ordovician age is further supported by observations of regional changes in metamorphic grade of especially the late Proterozoic Tapley Hill beds in the Adelaide “Geosyn- cline” by McKirdy et al. (1975). Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). From a detailed interpretation of the magnetic anomalies (Tucker, 1972), two stages of acquisition of secondary remanent magnetization were identified. Before folding, the beds acquired a remanent magnetic component close to the plane of sedimentary layering in a direc- tion 135” _+1 0. After folding another secondary magnetic component was imposed, again close to the bedding but in a general direction normal to the trace of outcrop. The agreement both in time of acquisition and in direction of McKirdy et al’s (1975) earlier mentioned secondary magnetic component with the characteristic component B is striking.
