INTERPRETATION A major problem during thermal analysis of especially the carbonate specimens was excessive increase in susceptibility and in VRM (Fig. 1.6T, U, V,) at temperatures well above 400°C. This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). It is well known (Dunlop, 1972) that newly formed magnetic phases may acquire a magnetization in absence of an ambient magnetic field, because of exchange coupling with the o

case of carbonate samples with a weak initial intensity which are subsequently further reduced during the demagnetization process, formation of such a secondary magnetic component may make it impossible to determine the primary magnetic component. Most red-bed samples showed an increase in susceptibility (Fig. 1.6R) after prolonged heating at temperatures above 500-6OO”C. A notable exception were red-bed samples from the Parachilna Formation and from the top member of the Billy Creek Formation (Fig. 1.6S, Table 1.4), which showed a significant decrease in susceptibility after heating above 400°C. This may be due to inversion of m~haemite to haematite (Turner and Ixer, 1977). The individual behaviour of the specimens during thermal demagnetiza- tion was variable (Fig. 1.5). It was often found that specimens taken from the same sample showed widely different blocking temperature regions for magnetic components of similar direction. This may partly be due to initial presence of an intimate mixture of authigenic magnetic minerals (Larson and Walker, 1975) further enhanced by a large variability in thermomagnetic properties of the transformed phase upon oxidation (Ryabushkin, 1976). Therefore, I prefer to treat the specimen directions as the fundamental unit for calculation of mean directions

Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). It is well known (Dunlop, 1972) that newly formed magnetic phases may acquire a magnetization in absence of an ambient magnetic field, because of exchange coupling with the o

case of carbonate samples with a weak initial intensity which are subsequently further reduced during the demagnetization process, formation of such a secondary magnetic component may make it impossible to determine the primary magnetic component. Most red-bed samples showed an increase in susceptibility (Fig. 1.6R) after prolonged heating at temperatures above 500-6OO”C. A notable exception were red-bed samples from the Parachilna Formation and from the top member of the Billy Creek Formation (Fig. 1.6S, Table 1.4), which showed a significant decrease in susceptibility after heating above 400°C. This may be due to inversion of m~haemite to haematite (Turner and Ixer, 1977). The individual behaviour of the specimens during thermal demagnetiza- tion was variable (Fig. 1.5). It was often found that specimens taken from the same sample showed widely different blocking temperature regions for magnetic components of similar direction. This may partly be due to initial presence of an intimate mixture of authigenic magnetic minerals (Larson and Walker, 1975) further enhanced by a large variability in thermomagnetic properties of the transformed phase upon oxidation (Ryabushkin, 1976). Therefore, I prefer to treat the specimen directions as the fundamental unit for calculation of mean directions

The occasional presence of both normal and reversed polarities of the same magnetic component in the same specimen (Fig. 1.7A), points to a fairly long period of acquisition of the characteristic magnetic component spanning at least the period of one polarity reversal. Such a prolonged acquisition of magnetization may be due to the formation of authigenic oxyhydroxides and haematite during diagenesis, and later dehydration and oxidation due to changes in Eh-Ph conditions and/or tectonic and thermo- chemical effects. For instance, Dijksman (1977) observed in Miocene red clay beds from central Spain that the same magnetic direction resided in both magnetite and a haematite magnetic phase. The latter was acquired with a time lag of several 100.000 yrs due to the effect of changing Eh-Ph condition in the CRM formation process. Cambrian-Early Ordovician age is further supported by observations of regional changes in metamorphic grade of especially the late Proterozoic Tapley Hill beds in the Adelaide “Geosyn- cline” by McKirdy et al. (1975). Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). From a detailed interpretation of the magnetic anomalies (Tucker, 1972), two stages of acquisition of secondary remanent magnetization were identified. Before folding, the beds acquired a remanent magnetic component close to the plane of sedimentary layering in a direc- tion 135” _+1 0. After folding another secondary magnetic component was imposed, again close to the bedding but in a general direction normal to the trace of outcrop. The agreement both in time of acquisition and in direction of McKirdy et al’s (1975) earlier mentioned secondary magnetic component with the characteristic component B is striking.

Cambrian results from the Flinders Ranges, South Australia INTRODUCTION Late Proterozoic and early Phanerozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Gondwanaland continents were reinterpreted recently by McElhinny et al. (19’7413) and McElhinny and Embleton (1976). Using selected pole positions, they showed that a common apparent polar wanderpath (APW) can be drawn when the main Gondwanaland fragments are reunited into the Smith and Hallam (1970) reconstruction. This common APW stretches from the ultimate Late Jurassic breakup backwards to at least 750 m.y. ago, thus implying unity of Gondwanaland during this period. Their proposed APW (south poles) has the shape of double question mark; one half spanning the late Proterozoic and the other half spanning the early Phanerozoic. The overall structure of this APW is certainly acceptable, but detailed examination indicates several discrepancies which make their proposed APW open to improvement and reinterpretation. Their proposed APW (south poles) has the shape of double question mark; one half spanning the late Proterozoic and the other half spanning the early Phanerozoic. The overall structure of this APW is certainly acceptable, but detailed examination indicates several discrepancies which make their proposed APW open to improvement and reinterpretation. One of the major uncertainties in constructing APW’s which span periods of appreciable polar movement is the inherent difficulty in assigning poles to either the normal or the reversed polarity group. McElhinny et al.% interpretation of polarities presently seems to be the more viable and less complicated approach. Cambrian results from the Flinders Ranges, South Australia INTRODUCTION Late Proterozoic and early Phanerozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Gondwanaland continents were reinterpreted recently by McElhinny et al. (19’7413) and McElhinny and Embleton (1976). Using selected pole positions, they showed that a common apparent polar wanderpath (APW) can be drawn when the main Gondwanaland fragments are reunited into the Smith and Hallam (1970) reconstruction. This common APW stretches from the ultimate Late Jurassic breakup backwards to at least 750 m.y. ago, thus implying unity of Gondwanaland during this period. Their proposed APW (south poles) has the shape of double question mark; one half spanning the late Proterozoic and the other half spanning the early Phanerozoic. The overall structure of this APW is certainly acceptable, but detailed examination indicates several discrepancies which make their proposed APW open to improvement and reinterpretation. The overall structure of this APW is certainly acceptable, but detailed examination indicates several discrepancies which make their proposed APW open to improvement and reinterpretation. One of the major uncertainties in constructing APW’s which span periods of appreciable polar movement is the inherent difficulty in assigning poles to either the normal or the reversed polarity group. McElhinny et al.% interpretation of polarities presently seems to be the more viable and less complicated approach. However, alternative backwards continuations of the Gondwanaland APW from its well defined late Palaeozoic trajectory, by reversing polarity of early Phanerozoic and latest Proterozoic palaeomagnetic poles (Piper, 1973; Schmidt and Morris, 1977) certainly cannot be ruled out. More palaeomagnetic poles are required in the less densely populated trajec- tories of appreciable polar wandering to solve this polarity ambiguity and for a better definition of the Gondwanaland APW. Samples were taken either as separate sites generally consisting of 6-8 samples or, if conditions permitted, as stratigraphic profiles with each sample taken from a separate bed at regular 1-2 m intervals. Stratigraphic intervals were measured with a Jacob’s Staff and an attached Abney level. Mostly two specimens, 2.5 cm diameter and 2.25 cm height, were sliced from each core. Up to three specimens from each site, or one specimen from each third sample in case of stratigraphic profiles, have been subjected to progressive thermal demagnetization studies. The heatings were done in air in a furnace described by McElhinny et al. (1971). Because of the complexity of magne- tization, all pilot specimens were progressively demagnetized in 12-18 steps with decreasing temperature intervals up to 685°C. The remaining specimens were subjected to partial progressive demag- 258 netization in 8-12 steps over a selected temperature interval. INTERPRETATION A major problem during thermal analysis of especially the carbonate specimens was excessive increase in susceptibility and in VRM (Fig. 1.6T, U, V,) at temperatures well above 400°C. This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). Cambrian-Early Ordovician age is further supported by observations of regional changes in metamorphic grade of especially the late Proterozoic Tapley Hill beds in the Adelaide “Geosyn- cline” by McKirdy et al. (1975). Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). From a detailed interpretation of the magnetic anomalies (Tucker, 1972), two stages of acquisition of secondary remanent magnetization were identified. Before folding, the beds acquired a remanent magnetic component close to the plane of sedimentary layering in a direc- tion 135” _+1 0. After folding another secondary magnetic component was imposed, again close to the bedding but in a general direction normal to the trace of outcrop. The agreement both in time of acquisition and in direction of McKirdy et al’s (1975) earlier mentioned secondary magnetic component with the characteristic component B is striking.

INTERPRETATION A major problem during thermal analysis of especially the carbonate specimens was excessive increase in susceptibility and in VRM (Fig. 1.6T, U, V,) at temperatures well above 400°C. This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). It is well known (Dunlop, 1972) that newly formed magnetic phases may acquire a magnetization in absence of an ambient magnetic field, because of exchange coupling with the o

Cambrian-Early Ordovician age is further supported by observations of regional changes in metamorphic grade of especially the late Proterozoic Tapley Hill beds in the Adelaide “Geosyn- cline” by McKirdy et al. (1975). Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). From a detailed interpretation of the magnetic anomalies (Tucker, 1972), two stages of acquisition of secondary remanent magnetization were identified. Before folding, the beds acquired a remanent magnetic component close to the plane of sedimentary layering in a direc- tion 135” _+1 0. After folding another secondary magnetic component was imposed, again close to the bedding but in a general direction normal to the trace of outcrop. The agreement both in time of acquisition and in direction of McKirdy et al’s (1975) earlier mentioned secondary magnetic component with the characteristic component B is striking.

Such a prolonged acquisition of magnetization may be due to the formation of authigenic oxyhydroxides and haematite during diagenesis, and later dehydration and oxidation due to changes in Eh-Ph conditions and/or tectonic and thermo- chemical effects. For instance, Dijksman (1977) observed in Miocene red clay beds from central Spain that the same magnetic direction resided in both magnetite and a haematite magnetic phase. The latter was acquired with a time lag of several 100.000 yrs due to the effect of changing Eh-Ph condition in the CRM formation process. Dual polarity observations were also made in Billy Creek equivalent beds on Kangaroo Island and in some sequences in the Amadeus Basin (Section III). In the latter basin, specimens from red beds in a Middle Cambrian section near Areyonga showed components of dual polarity, whereas time equivalent rocks of a carbonate sequence near Ross River did not show this effect. Dual polarity observations were also made in Billy Creek equivalent beds on Kangaroo Island and in some sequences in the Amadeus Basin (Section III). In the latter basin, specimens from red beds in a Middle Cambrian section near Areyonga showed components of dual polarity, whereas time equivalent rocks of a carbonate sequence near Ross River did not show this effect. Clearly, such a prolonged period of acquisition of magnetization, leading occasionally in red beds to a dual polarity, questions the suitability of such thermally demagnetized red beds results for magnetostratigraphic studies. Chemical demagnetization may prove to be more successful in those cases where early and late diagenetic magnetization components can be separated on the basis of distinct chemical properties (Roy and Park, 1974), but has not been undertaken in the course of the present study. A comparison with the mean Gondwanaland data points to the SSW-SW directed magnetic component (A) as the primary magnetization. Its direc- tion shows a minor gradual change through the stratigraphical sequence as will be discussed (Table I.1). I interpret the WNW-NNW aligned charac- teristic magnetic component (B) as a secondary magnetization which pre- dates regional folding of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” sediments during the 273 Late Cambrian-Early Ordovician Delamarian Orogeny. Samples were taken either as separate sites generally consisting of 6-8 samples or, if conditions permitted, as stratigraphic profiles with each sample taken from a separate bed at regular 1-2 m intervals. Stratigraphic intervals were measured with a Jacob’s Staff and an attached Abney level. Mostly two specimens, 2.5 cm diameter and 2.25 cm height, were sliced from each core. Up to three specimens from each site, or one specimen from each third sample in case of stratigraphic profiles, have been subjected to progressive thermal demagnetization studies. The heatings were done in air in a furnace described by McElhinny et al. (1971). Because of the complexity of magne- tization, all pilot specimens were progressively demagnetized in 12-18 steps with decreasing temperature intervals up to 685°C. The intensity of suscep- tibility was measured after each heating step on a Digico bulk susceptibility unit. The remaining specimens were subjected to partial progressive demag- 258 netization in 8-12 steps over a selected temperature interval. Care was taken to keep the specimens in a very much reduced magnetic environment since the specimens tended to acquire Viscous Remanent Magnetization
